claims.text: Q235 steel in the as-received state is a low-carbon steel.
Annealing Q235 steel at 750 °C for 1–2 hours in 2–5% O2 in N2 with controlled cooling will reproducibly form the intended oxide layer.
Controlled annealing in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere will form a continuous, Fe3O4-rich scale on Q235 steel.
The Fe3O4-rich scale acts as an effective diffusion barrier.
A continuous, predominant Fe3O4 layer minimizes ingress of aggressive ionic species.
Fe2O3 is less protective than Fe3O4 in the proposed corrosion regime.
A porous or cracked Fe2O3-dominated scale permits accelerated high-temperature corrosive attack.
The Fe3O4-rich scale will significantly reduce high-temperature corrosion during Na2SO4/V2O5 salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
Annealed samples with a continuous Fe3O4-rich scale will exhibit less mass change than unannealed Q235 controls during high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed samples with a continuous Fe3O4-rich scale will retain mechanical properties better than unannealed Q235 controls during high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealing-induced oxide formation will have minimal effect on Q235 corrosion performance under room-temperature humidity conditions.
Formation of a non-protective oxide layer will accelerate corrosion.
The proposed protective mechanism applies specifically to salt-containing environments at 700–900 °C.
The protective role may be insignificant when oxide formation occurs under substantially different oxygen partial pressures or thermal histories.
The intended oxide phase distribution is sensitive to oxide-formation kinetics and may not be reproducible.
Minor processing variations can alter the balance of oxide phases.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes annealing 'pre-exposed Q235 steel,' whereas the stated initial state is pre-exposure, as-received Q235 steel.
